why_this_tool: PostgreSQL runs free on a laptop, offers several index types on one heap-based B-tree engine, and exposes both its multiversion behaviour and its real query plans through EXPLAIN, so every claim in the lesson can be checked by hand.
alternatives: MySQL InnoDB is also a B-tree engine but clusters rows by primary key; RocksDB and Apache Cassandra use LSM-trees that favour write throughput and pay with compaction and slower reads; SQLite is an embedded single-file B-tree engine with no server process; Amazon S3 is object storage with no secondary indexes or query planner.

setup.do: Install PostgreSQL 18 on your laptop with your package manager or as a local container; no cloud account or GPU is needed.
setup.done_when: Asking the server for its version returns a PostgreSQL 18 version string.
setup.why: Every later step runs against a local server whose version matches the documentation you will cite.

setup.do: Start the server, connect with the psql client, and create an empty practice database for this lesson.
setup.done_when: The psql prompt shows the practice database name and listing its tables returns none.
setup.why: A dedicated database lets you drop and rebuild tables and indexes freely without touching anything else.

setup.do: Create an orders table with an id, a customer id, a status, a timestamp and a text column, load a few million generated rows, then run ANALYZE on it.
setup.done_when: A row count on the table returns the number of rows you generated and the load took long enough to notice.
setup.why: Plans only become interesting when the table is too big to scan cheaply, and the planner needs fresh statistics to estimate row counts.

steps.do: Run EXPLAIN on a query that selects one customer's orders from the table while it has no index.
steps.done_when: The output shows a Seq Scan node with a startup cost, a total cost and an estimated row count that you can each explain.
steps.why: This is the first run: you see the plan tree, the sequential scan node and the cost and row estimates before any tuning.

steps.do: Create a default B-tree index on the customer id column and run the same EXPLAIN again.
steps.done_when: The plan switches from a Seq Scan to an Index Scan or Bitmap Heap Scan and the total cost estimate drops.
steps.why: The B-tree is the default index structure and the core of this engine family, so you should watch it change the access path.

steps.do: Run a timed bulk insert into the table with no secondary indexes, then repeat it with four B-tree indexes in place, and compare the timings.
steps.done_when: You have two recorded timings and can state in one sentence why an LSM-tree engine would absorb the same writes differently and what it pays on reads.
steps.why: Every B-tree index is updated in place on each write, which is the cost that LSM-tree engines such as RocksDB and Cassandra avoid by appending and compacting later.

steps.do: Create a hash index, a GIN index on a text search or array column, and a BRIN index on the timestamp column, then compare their sizes with the B-tree.
steps.done_when: You have a small table of index type, size on disk and which query operators it can serve, filled in from your own database.
steps.why: Each index type supports different operators and has a very different size and maintenance cost, so the choice is part of design.

steps.do: Create a multicolumn index, a partial index on one status value, an expression index on lowercased text, and a covering index with an included column.
steps.done_when: For each of the four indexes you have one query whose plan uses it and one similar query whose plan does not, and you can say why.
steps.why: Index design is about matching the shape of real queries: column order, predicates and included columns decide whether an index is usable at all.

steps.do: Run EXPLAIN with the ANALYZE and BUFFERS options on your queries and compare estimated rows with actual rows at every node.
steps.done_when: You can point to one node where the estimate and the actual row count differ and one where buffer counts show the work done.
steps.why: Estimates are guesses; only the executed plan shows real timings, loop counts and how many pages were read from cache or disk.

steps.do: Query the table with a very selective filter, a moderately selective filter and a filter matching most rows, and compare the three plans.
steps.done_when: You have seen all three scan types on the same column and can say roughly at what selectivity the planner switched.
steps.why: The planner picks an index scan, a bitmap scan or a sequential scan depending on selectivity, and reading that choice is the heart of plan reading.

steps.do: Start two psql sessions, open a repeatable read transaction in one, update and commit rows in the other, and query from both.
steps.done_when: The first session still returns the old values until its transaction ends, and neither session waited on the other.
steps.why: Multiversion concurrency means readers see a snapshot and do not block writers, and watching two sessions disagree makes that concrete.

steps.do: Run a large update across the table while an old transaction stays open, then measure the table and index sizes and check the dead tuple count before and after a VACUUM.
steps.done_when: You see the table grow, dead tuples that VACUUM cannot remove while the old transaction is open, and their removal once it is closed.
steps.why: The cost of multiversion storage is that old row versions stay on disk until no snapshot needs them, which bloats tables and indexes.

steps.do: Run a query that should be an index-only scan right after heavy updates and again after VACUUM, comparing the Heap Fetches figure in each plan.
steps.done_when: The Heap Fetches number is high after the updates and near zero after VACUUM for the same query.
steps.why: This ties the subtopics together: row versions force the engine back to the heap for visibility checks, and the plan output proves it.

steps.do: Configure a production-like run: start a sustained concurrent read and write load with pgbench, build a new index concurrently while it runs, then query the index usage statistics and drop any index that was never scanned.
steps.done_when: The load kept committing transactions during the index build, and you have a list of indexes with their scan counts and at least one keep or drop decision justified by it.
steps.why: In production you add indexes without blocking writers and you prune the ones that cost writes without serving reads.
